title: Introduction to Parallel and Distributed Programming using N-Body Simulations
problem: Students struggle to understand parallel and distributed programming concepts in abstract terms. N-body simulations provide a concrete, visually compelling problem that demonstrates algorithmic complexity, scaling challenges, and practical parallelization strategies from basic to advanced levels.
motivation: Parallel and distributed programming expertise is crucial for HPC and modern scientific computing, but traditional teaching methods often lack the visual and practical engagement needed for deep understanding.
method: The curriculum teaches parallelization concepts through n-body simulations (calculating how many objects move under each other's gravitational forces). Bachelor students code galaxy collisions in C++ using Git and remote development, which teaches them how code complexity grows as problems get bigger. Master students parallelize solar system simulations using OpenMP (to speed up code by splitting the work within one computer) and MPI (to speed up code by splitting work across many computers), with the option to add GPU acceleration, molecular dynamics simulations, and interactive visualization.
key_novelty: N-body simulations form a single educational framework that teaches sequential programming, parallelization, and distributed computing through a visually compelling problem.
contributions: Structured two-tier curriculum using n-body simulations to teach parallel and distributed programming
Integration of practical tools and environments (Git, C++, OpenMP, MPI, GPU computing) into coherent learning pathway
Publicly available, instructor-adaptable course materials and curriculum design
Demonstration that visual, mathematically grounded problems improve learning outcomes for complex programming concepts
limitations: Not discussed in abstract; no quantitative evaluation of educational effectiveness reported
